You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: transform the black DVD into a white DVD
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the object matched to the source DVD remain identifiable as that DVD after the edit?
node.criteria: Pass if the matched object remains identifiable as a DVD; fail if it is no longer identifiable as a DVD; unknown if the object's correspondence to the source DVD or its DVD identity cannot be determined.
node.binding: Assess DVD identity for the specific object tracked from the source image using shape, location, and surrounding context. Do not infer identity solely because an edited object is a white disc; report uncertainty if the source object cannot confidently be identified or matched.

node_traces.evidence: The source image contains a small rectangular-looking item near the center, but it is not clearly identifiable as a DVD. In the edited image, a white disc appears near that location, but the source object's DVD identity and correspondence cannot be confidently established from shape and context alone.

response.content: {"text":"The binding overweights uncertainty about whether the source item is truly a DVD and whether the edited disc is the same object. The source image shows a small rectangular, printed item near the center; the edit shows a white disc at that location, while a separate white disc appears on the dark object to the right. This is evidence of a likely transformation, but the trace does not establish which disc corresponds to the source item. Keep identity and correspondence as distinct checks: assess spatial/scene correspondence and visible change, and use unknown only when those cannot be resolved—not merely because the source is not unmistakably a DVD. Conversely, do not treat a nearby white disc alone as proof of a successful edit. The reference “no” is an aggregate constraint, not atomic ground truth; the rubric’s “no progress” versus “partial progress” distinction may be ambiguous here, so inspect whether the node’s criterion captures requested progress rather than only post-edit DVD identity. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is reported; this is a visual-evidence and criterion-resolution issue."}
